summary: Gives guidance to content providers and application service providers who wish to serve both IPv6 and IPv4 customers. Many points also apply to hosting providers and enterprise networks preparing for IPv6 users. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A shop owner's guide to opening a second door for customers who arrive from the new road, while keeping the old door open too.

questions: how to make a website ipv6 ready
how to deploy ipv6 for a content provider
subtitle: How content providers can serve IPv6 customers alongside IPv4

tldr.problem: Content and application providers built entirely on IPv4 face a complex task: enabling IPv6 service without breaking IPv4 customers or requiring a complete overhaul.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides practical guidance across infrastructure, operations, and strategy, covering DNS, load balancers, proxies, servers, and the transition technologies some customers will still use.
tldr.outcome: Providers can achieve dual-stack service through careful planning, staff training, staged rollout, and choosing between outside-in or inside-out deployment strategies.

today: RFC 6883 remains a foundational guide for IPv6 deployment in production environments, though some specific technologies and timelines have evolved since 2013. It is not obsoleted and remains widely referenced by deploying organizations.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Matters Now
sections.content:
By 2013, when this RFC was written, the central IPv4 address registry (IANA) had exhausted its free blocks, and regional registries were expected to run dry within one or two years. This meant that ISPs would soon stop handing out IPv4 addresses to new customers. Some of those customers would eventually connect via IPv6-only connections or dual-stack where IPv6 is preferred. For content providers, the message was urgent: start now while IPv6-only customers are few, so you can scale gracefully rather than rushing later.

The document targets Internet Content Providers (ICPs) and Application Service Providers (ASPs) who currently support only IPv4. It acknowledges that deploying a second network-layer protocol is unfamiliar territory for most organizations and requires deliberate strategy, not casual retrofitting.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 addresses were running out, so some customers would soon arrive only via IPv6. The time to prepare was before they came in large numbers.

sections.title: Dual-Stack Strategy and Deployment Approaches
sections.content:
The recommended strategy is dual-stack deployment: running both IPv4 and IPv6 equally on all services. This allows existing IPv4 customers to stay unaffected while new IPv6-only customers gain access. However, deploying dual-stack is not a single project; it must be coordinated across infrastructure, applications, and operations.

The RFC describes two sequencing approaches. The outside-in approach starts by putting an IPv6 proxy or load balancer in front of existing IPv4 servers, giving external customers IPv6 access immediately while internal systems migrate gradually. The inside-out approach builds internal IPv6 support first, then exposes IPv6 to external customers once internal systems are mature. Each approach has trade-offs: outside-in gives early customer access and operational experience; inside-out completes the deployment as a cohesive project.
sections.plainLanguage: You can either open the new door first and route customers through a translator to the old rooms, or renovate all the inside first and then open both doors at once.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Network Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC covers address assignment, routing, and DNS. Large providers should decide whether to obtain a Provider-Independent (PI) prefix directly from regional registries (enabling portability if they change ISPs) or use Provider Aggregated (PA) prefixes from their ISPs (the more common approach). Both are viable but have different implications for multi-ISP scenarios.

Routing in dual-stack networks requires all providers to deploy IPv6 versions of their routing protocols (OSPFv3, IS-IS, RIPng). The RFC advises evaluating firmware requirements and performance impacts. For DNS, a critical requirement is that every externally visible host with an A record for IPv4 must have a AAAA record for IPv6 before that record is published; publishing broken AAAA records breaks the service for IPv6 users. Additionally, DNS servers should respond to queries over both IPv4 and IPv6, since some clients can only resolve names via IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to number your new IPv6 rooms, set up the routing so mail goes to both sides, and make sure your address book (DNS) works when customers call from either IPv4 or IPv6.

sections.title: Application and Operations Readiness
sections.content:
Server application stacks (HTTP, email, etc.) have supported IPv6 for years, but ASPs must test applications in IPv4-only, IPv6-only, and dual-stack environments before enabling production dual-stack. Cookie-based authentication needs careful redesign, since clients may use either IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, and with privacy addressing, IPv6 addresses can change frequently. Applications should use domain names, not IP addresses. Logging systems need to handle IPv6 addresses. Geolocation services will initially be weak for IPv6 but are expected to improve.

Staff training is critical and often overlooked. All staff—from architects to help desk—need to understand IPv6, not just one designated expert. Training should be timed just before deployment to stick in memory. Load balancers and proxies must be tested for IPv6 support and performance before deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Your websites, staff, and tools all need to know about IPv6. Test everything, retrain everyone, and don't try to be perfect—just get it working.

sections.title: Coping with Transition and Long-Term Realities
sections.content:
Some customers will inevitably connect via IPv6-to-IPv4 translators (NAT64) or IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels if they lack native IPv6 or if providers fail to give them IPv6 access. The RFC recommends providers ensure Path MTU Discovery works (ICMP is not blocked), since tunneled traffic may have smaller MTU than native IPv6. Dual-stack providers should not receive much translator traffic, since they offer both A and AAAA records.

The RFC notes that some providers use interim solutions like DNS whitelisting (hiding AAAA records from clients with broken IPv6) or IPv6-only subdomains for testing. These are temporary expedients, not long-term solutions. The document recommends the Happy Eyeballs approach (RFC 6555), which lets clients gracefully fall back if one address family fails. Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) must support full dual-stack at all points of presence, not just some; partial IPv6 support wastes deployment effort.
sections.plainLanguage: Some customers will come through tunnels or translators. Make sure those work, but focus on direct IPv6. Eventually everyone will have IPv6, so design for that future.

sections.title: Key Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC synthesizes its guidance into actionable recommendations. First, have a deliberate strategy for when and how to enable IPv6; do not attempt it casually. Second, ensure every staff member with IPv4 knowledge also has IPv6 knowledge; education is non-negotiable. Third, verify that hardware vendors have concrete plans to support IPv6 with equivalent performance. Fourth, obtain native IPv6 connectivity from ISPs, not tunnels; tunnels introduce latency and MTU issues. Fifth, use DNS and service discovery rather than hardcoded addresses, a practice that serves both IPv4 and IPv6 well. Sixth, test thoroughly in isolated lab environments before production deployment.

The overall message is that while IPv6 deployment is substantial work, it is manageable with discipline, planning, and proper sequencing. Complacency in 2013 risked losing market share as IPv6-only customers appeared.
sections.plainLanguage: Plan ahead, train your team, get real IPv6 from your ISP, test everything in a lab first, and design as if IPv4 were already gone.
